behavior_items: The reproducer compares three equivalent ways to compute the count of redundant sign bits for a signed long: a manual decomposition through count-leading-zeros in clrsb1, a bit-manipulation form tailored to __builtin_clzl in clrsb2, and the direct builtin __builtin_clrsbl in clrsb3.

The macro SHIFT expands to sizeof(x)*8-1 inside each function body, so for a long operand it becomes the index of the sign bit. Shifting x right by SHIFT produces either all zeros for nonnegative values or all ones for negative values, assuming the target's arithmetic right shift used by GCC for signed values in this context.

Function clz wraps __builtin_clzl with explicit zero handling. This matters because the C builtin for count-leading-zeros is undefined for zero at the language level, while the wrapper defines the result as the bit width of unsigned long.

Function clsb computes clz(x ^ (x >> SHIFT)). The xor with the sign-bit replica normalizes the input so that values with leading copies of the sign bit become values with leading zeros. For nonnegative x, x >> SHIFT is 0 and clsb becomes clz(x). For negative x, x >> SHIFT is -1 and clsb becomes clz(~x). This yields the number of leading sign bits including the sign bit itself.
Function clrsb1 returns clsb(x) - 1, converting the count from 'leading sign bits including the sign bit' to the standard clrsb meaning 'redundant sign bits excluding the sign bit'.

Function clrsb2 uses the identity ((x << 1) ^ (x >> SHIFT)) | 1 before applying __builtin_clzl. Left shifting by one discards the original sign bit, xor with the sign-fill pattern turns a negative input into the complement of that shifted value, and forcing the low bit to 1 guarantees a nonzero argument so __builtin_clzl can be used safely without a branch or wrapper.

The or-with-1 in clrsb2 is specifically aimed at targets where the lowering of count-leading-zeros relies on an instruction like x86 BSR, whose behavior for zero is unsuitable. By guaranteeing a nonzero input, GCC can emit a straight-line sequence without a zero check.

The bug report notes that GCC does optimize the hand-written formulations clrsb1 or clrsb2 into efficient target instructions/sequences, but does not similarly inline or lower __builtin_clrsbl in clrsb3 on some targets. Thus the reproducer is about missed expansion of a builtin, not a wrong numeric result.
On AArch64, GCC recognizes __builtin_clrsbl and lowers it to the target cls instruction, which directly counts leading sign bits. This is the expected ideal behavior the report uses as a reference.

On 32-bit ARM, the report says GCC fails to inline __builtin_clrsbl, yet the manual clrsb1 form is optimized to a compact sequence using arithmetic shift, xor, clz, and subtract. This demonstrates that the backend can synthesize the operation efficiently even though the builtin expansion path is missing or not selected.

The ARM sequence shown for clrsb1 performs exactly the source-level transformation: xor the value with its sign-filled right shift, count leading zeros with clz, then subtract one to exclude the sign bit from the final count.

On x86/Intel, the report says GCC also does not inline __builtin_clrsbl, while the clrsb2 source form becomes a short sequence using lea for x<<1, sar for sign replication, xor/or normalization, bsr for finding the highest set bit, and xor with 63 to convert the bit index into a leading-zero count on 64-bit long.

The x86 sequence reflects target-specific constraints: unlike ARM clz, BSR does not define a useful result for zero, so the compiler benefits from the clrsb2 formulation's guaranteed nonzero operand. This explains why the reproducer includes two different hand-written variants and why one is preferred on Intel.

The behavior exercised is therefore target-dependent builtin lowering. The reproducer asks the compiler to optimize semantically equivalent formulations and exposes that GCC's general optimization pipeline can recognize and streamline the manual idioms, but the dedicated __builtin_clrsbl path is not consistently expanded on ARM 32-bit and x86 under -O3.

Because all three functions are simple and side-effect free, the test is focused entirely on code generation quality: whether the compiler emits inline arithmetic/bit-manipulation instructions or leaves a less optimal call/sequence for __builtin_clrsbl.

The reproducer implicitly checks that GCC understands value-range and bit-level identities across signed and unsigned operations, especially arithmetic right shift, xor normalization, zero handling for clz, and conversion between count-leading-sign-bits and count-leading-zeros.

A key compiler-behavior contrast in the reproducer is that pattern recognition of ordinary C code appears stronger than builtin expansion for this operation on the affected targets. That is the essence of the bug report's complaint that '__builtin_clrsb is never inlined' there.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer evaluates GCC's code generation for counting redundant sign bits of a signed long. It presents two manual implementations, clrsb1 and clrsb2, that reduce the problem to count-leading-zeros, plus the direct builtin form clrsb3 using __builtin_clrsbl. clrsb1 computes clz(x ^ signmask) - 1, while clrsb2 transforms the input to a guaranteed nonzero value so __builtin_clzl can be lowered efficiently even on targets like x86 where the underlying BSR instruction does not handle zero well. According to the report, GCC at -O3 successfully optimizes the manual C formulations into efficient inline instruction sequences on ARM 32-bit and x86, but fails to inline or directly lower __builtin_clrsbl on those targets, even though it does so on AArch64 via the cls instruction. The reproducer therefore exposes a missed optimization or missing target expansion for the clrsb builtin rather than a semantic miscompile.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a target-dependent missed lowering of the redundant-sign-bit-count builtin rather than any semantic problem in the source. The reproducer shows that GCC can already optimize equivalent hand-written expressions into efficient inline sequences on ARM32 and x86: on ARM via arithmetic shift + xor + clz + subtract, and on x86 via shift/xor/or plus bsr-based leading-zero computation. AArch64 lowers the builtin directly to a dedicated cls instruction, so the failure is not in generic semantics of __builtin_clrsbl itself but in how GCC expands or recognizes it on specific back ends. This strongly suggests a defect in builtin expansion, optab selection, or combine/match logic for CLRSB on ARM32 and x86, where the direct builtin path is not mapped to either a target instruction or a synthesized RTL sequence even though equivalent idioms are optimized successfully. Another recurring pattern is zero-handling: the manual x86 form explicitly guarantees a nonzero operand before __builtin_clzl because bsr is problematic on zero. That implies GCC may lack a canonical fallback expansion for clrsb that preserves semantics while accounting for target-specific clz/bsr zero behavior. Overall, the bug is most consistent with missing or disabled expansion patterns for CLRSB in the middle end or machine descriptions, or missed canonicalization from CLRSB to recognized CLZ-based forms during optimization.
possible_causes: Missing target-specific expansion for the CLRSB builtin/optab on ARM 32-bit and x86, causing __builtin_clrsbl to remain as a libcall or non-inlined builtin while AArch64 has a proper direct lowering.

The middle-end expansion for CLRSB is incomplete: GCC does not rewrite __builtin_clrsbl into the equivalent normalized CLZ-based expression (such as clz(x ^ (x >> (W-1))) - 1 or the nonzero-safe variant) on targets lacking a native clrsb instruction.

Machine description or RTL pattern support for sign-bit-count is absent or not hooked up for SImode/DImode on the affected targets, so instruction selection cannot match the builtin even though later combines can optimize hand-written idioms.

A missed canonicalization/combine issue: ordinary C expressions are recognized and simplified into clz/bsr sequences, but the direct CLRSB internal representation is not converted into forms that existing combine or match.pd rules know how to optimize.

Incorrect cost modeling or expansion policy for the builtin may suppress inline expansion on ARM32/x86, preferring a fallback helper path even under -O3 despite a cheaper synthesized sequence being available.

Target-specific zero-handling concerns for CLZ/BSR may have prevented GCC from enabling a generic CLRSB expansion; the compiler may lack the safe fallback logic needed to transform CLRSB into a nonzero-guaranteed CLZ/BSR sequence on x86.

A mode/precision bug in builtin handling for long-sized operands could prevent __builtin_clrsbl from selecting the right expansion on ILP32 ARM and LP64 x86-64, even though equivalent source expressions optimize after normal scalar transformations.

The manual implementation clrsb1 is optimized on ARM32 to 'xor with sign-fill, clz, subtract 1', proving GCC can generate an efficient inline sequence for the operation when expressed indirectly.
The manual implementation clrsb2 is optimized on x86 to a compact lea/sar/xor/or/bsr/xor sequence, proving the backend and optimizer already support the needed primitive operations.

Because the same builtin lowers correctly on AArch64 but not on ARM32/x86, the defect is likely in per-target machine descriptions, optab wiring, or target-specific expansion hooks rather than the front-end parsing of the builtin.

(If the clz instruction produces the usual value at 0, which is K, the result of this code sequence will be -1; expand_ffs, below, relies on this. gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function tries to implement an atomic exchange operation using a compare_and_swap loop. VAL is written to *MEM. The previous contents of MEM are returned, using TARGET if possible. No memory model is required since a compare_and_swap loop is seq-cst.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static rtx maybe_emit_atomic_test_and_set (rtx target, rtx mem, enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function tries to implement an atomic test-and-set operation using the atomic_test_and_set instruction pattern. A boolean value is returned from the operation, using TARGET if possible.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_sync_lock_test_and_set (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the legacy _sync_lock test_and_set operation which is generally an atomic exchange. Some limited targets only allow the constant 1 to be stored. This is an ACQUIRE operation. TARGET is an optional place to stick the return value. MEM is where VAL is stored.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_atomic_test_and_set (rtx target, rtx mem, enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the atomic test_and_set operation: atomically store a boolean TRUE into MEM and return the previous value. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. TARGET is an optional place to stick the return value.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_atomic_exchange (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the atomic exchange operation: atomically store VAL in MEM and return the previous value in MEM. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. TARGET is an optional place to stick the return value.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool expand_atomic_compare_and_swap (rtx *ptarget_bool, rtx *ptarget_oval, rtx mem, rtx expected, rtx desired, bool is_weak, enum memmodel succ_model, enum memmodel fail_model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the atomic compare exchange operation: PTARGET_BOOL is an optional place to store the boolean success/failure. PTARGET_OVAL is an optional place to store the old value from memory. Both target parameters may be NULL or const0_rtx to indicate that we do not care about that return value. Both target parameters are updated on success to the actual location of the corresponding result. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. The return value of the function is true for success.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static void expand_asm_memory_blockage (void)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Generate asm volatile("" : : : "memory") as the memory blockage.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static void expand_memory_blockage (void)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Do not propagate memory accesses across this point.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void expand_asm_reg_clobber_mem_blockage (HARD_REG_SET regs)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Generate asm volatile("" : : : "memory") as a memory blockage, at the same time clobbering the register set specified by REGS.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void expand_mem_thread_fence (enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This routine will either emit the mem_thread_fence pattern or issue a sync_synchronize to generate a fence for memory model MEMMODEL.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void expand_mem_signal_fence (enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Emit a signal fence with given memory model.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_atomic_load (rtx target, rtx mem, enum memmodel model)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the atomic load operation: return the atomically loaded value in MEM. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. TARGET is an option place to stick the return value.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_atomic_store (rtx mem, rtx val, enum memmodel model, bool use_release)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands the atomic store operation: Atomically store VAL in MEM. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. USE_RELEASE is true if __sync_lock_release can be used as a fall back. function returns const0_rtx if a pattern was emitted.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static void get_atomic_op_for_code (struct atomic_op_functions *op, enum rtx_code code)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Fill in structure pointed to by OP with the various optab entries for an operation of type CODE.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static rtx maybe_optimize_fetch_op (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum rtx_code code, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: See if there is a more optimal way to implement the operation "*MEM CODE VAL" using memory order MODEL. If AFTER is true the operation needs to return the value of *MEM after the operation, otherwise the previous value. TARGET is an optional place to place the result. The result is unused if it is const0_rtx. Return the result if there is a better sequence, otherwise NULL_RTX.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static rtx maybe_emit_op (const struct atomic_op_functions *optab, rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, bool use_memmodel, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Try to emit an instruction for a specific operation varaition. OPTAB contains the OP functions. TARGET is an optional place to return the result. const0_rtx means unused. MEM is the memory location to operate on. VAL is the value to use in the operation. USE_MEMMODEL is TRUE if the variation with a memory model should be tried. MODEL is the memory model, if used. AFTER is true if the returned result is the value after the operation.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static rtx expand_atomic_fetch_op_no_fallback (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum rtx_code code, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands an atomic fetch_OP or OP_fetch operation: TARGET is an option place to stick the return value. const0_rtx indicates the result is unused. atomically fetch MEM, perform the operation with VAL and return it to MEM. CODE is the operation being performed (OP) MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. AFTER is true to return the result of the operation (OP_fetch). AFTER is false to return the value before the operation (fetch_OP). This function will *only* generate instructions if there is a direct optab. No compare and swap loops or libcalls will be generated.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx expand_atomic_fetch_op (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum rtx_code code, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: This function expands an atomic fetch_OP or OP_fetch operation: TARGET is an option place to stick the return value. const0_rtx indicates the result is unused. atomically fetch MEM, perform the operation with VAL and return it to MEM. CODE is the operation being performed (OP) MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. AFTER is true to return the result of the operation (OP_fetch). AFTER is false to return the value before the operation (fetch_OP).

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool insn_operand_matches (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int opno, rtx operand)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Return true if OPERAND is suitable for operand number OPNO of instruction ICODE.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool valid_multiword_target_p (rtx target)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: TARGET is a target of a multiword operation that we are going to implement as a series of word-mode operations. Return true if TARGET is suitable for this purpose.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void create_integer_operand (class expand_operand *op, poly_int64 intval)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Make OP describe an input operand that has value INTVAL and that has no inherent mode. This function should only be used for operands that are always expand-time constants. The backend may request that INTVAL be copied into a different kind of rtx, but it must specify the mode of that rtx if so.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static bool maybe_legitimize_operand_same_code (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int opno, class expand_operand *op)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Like maybe_legitimize_operand, but do not change the code of the current rtx value.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static bool maybe_legitimize_operand (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int opno, class expand_operand *op)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Try to make OP match operand OPNO of instruction ICODE. Return true on success, storing the new operand value back in OP.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void create_convert_operand_from_type (class expand_operand *op, rtx value, tree type)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Make OP describe an input operand that should have the same value as VALUE, after any mode conversion that the target might request. TYPE is the type of VALUE.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: static inline bool can_reuse_operands_p (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int opno1, unsigned int opno2, const class expand_operand *op1, const class expand_operand *op2)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Return true if the requirements on operands OP1 and OP2 of instruction ICODE are similar enough for the result of legitimizing OP1 to be reusable for OP2. OPNO1 and OPNO2 are the operand numbers associated with OP1 and OP2 respectively.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool maybe_legitimize_operands (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int opno, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Try to make operands [OPS, OPS + NOPS) match operands [OPNO, OPNO + NOPS) of instruction ICODE. Return true on success, leaving the new operand values in the OPS themselves. Emit no code on failure.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: rtx_insn * maybe_gen_insn (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Try to generate instruction ICODE, using operands [OPS, OPS + NOPS) as its operands. Return the instruction pattern on success, and emit any necessary set-up code. Return null and emit no code on failure.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool maybe_expand_insn (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Try to emit instruction ICODE, using operands [OPS, OPS + NOPS) as its operands. Return true on success and emit no code on failure.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: bool maybe_expand_jump_insn (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Like maybe_expand_insn, but for jumps.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void expand_insn (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Emit instruction ICODE, using operands [OPS, OPS + NOPS) as its operands.

gcc/optabs.c.signature: void expand_jump_insn (enum insn_code icode, unsigned int nops, class expand_operand *ops)
gcc/optabs.c.summary: Like expand_insn, but for jumps.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static bool is_builtin_name (const char *name)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return true if NAME starts with __builtin_ or __sync_.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: bool called_as_built_in (tree node)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return true if NODE should be considered for inline expansion regardless of the optimization level. This means whenever a function is invoked with its "internal" name, which normally contains the prefix "__builtin".

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static bool get_object_alignment_2 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp, bool addr_p)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Compute values M and N such that M divides (address of EXP - N) and such that N < M. If these numbers can be determined, store M in alignp and N in BITPOSP and return true. Otherwise return false and store BITS_PER_UNIT to alignp and any bit-offset to *bitposp. Note that the address (and thus the alignment) computed here is based on the address to which a symbol resolves, whereas DECL_ALIGN is based on the address at which an object is actually located. These two addresses are not always the same. For example, on ARM targets, the address &foo of a Thumb function foo() has the lowest bit set, whereas foo() itself starts on an even address. If ADDR_P is true we are taking the address of the memory reference EXP and thus cannot rely on the access taking place.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: bool get_object_alignment_1 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: For a memory reference expression EXP compute values M and N such that M divides (&EXP - N) and such that N < M. If these numbers can be determined, store M in alignp and N in *BITPOSP and return true. Otherwise return false and store BITS_PER_UNIT to *alignp and any bit-offset to *bitposp.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: unsigned int get_object_alignment (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the alignment in bits of EXP, an object.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: bool get_pointer_alignment_1 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: For a pointer valued expression EXP compute values M and N such that M divides (EXP - N) and such that N < M. If these numbers can be determined, store M in alignp and N in *BITPOSP and return true. Return false if the results are just a conservative approximation. If EXP is not a pointer, false is returned too.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: unsigned int get_pointer_alignment (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the alignment in bits of EXP, a pointer valued expression. The alignment returned is, by default, the alignment of the thing that EXP points to. If it is not a POINTER_TYPE, 0 is returned. Otherwise, look at the expression to see if we can do better, i.e., if the expression is actually pointing at an object whose alignment is tighter.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: unsigned string_length (const void *ptr, unsigned eltsize, unsigned maxelts)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the number of leading non-zero elements in the sequence [ PTR, PTR + MAXELTS ) where each element's size is ELTSIZE bytes. ELTSIZE must be a power of 2 less than 8. Used by c_strlen.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: tree c_strlen (tree arg, int only_value, c_strlen_data *data, unsigned eltsize)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Compute the length of a null-terminated character string or wide character string handling character sizes of 1, 2, and 4 bytes. TREE_STRING_LENGTH is not the right way because it evaluates to the size of the character array in bytes (as opposed to characters) and because it can contain a zero byte in the middle. ONLY_VALUE should be nonzero if the result is not going to be emitted into the instruction stream and zero if it is going to be expanded. E.g. with i++ ? "foo" : "bar", if ONLY_VALUE is nonzero, constant 3 is returned, otherwise NULL, since len = c_strlen (ARG, 1); if (len) expand_expr (len, ...); would not evaluate the side-effects. If ONLY_VALUE is two then we do not emit warnings about out-of-bound accesses. Note that this implies the result is not going to be emitted into the instruction stream. Additional information about the string accessed may be recorded in DATA. For example, if ARG references an unterminated string, then the declaration will be stored in the DECL field. If the length of the unterminated string can be determined, it'll be stored in the LEN field. Note this length could well be different than what a C strlen call would return. ELTSIZE is 1 for norm

gcc/builtins.c.signature: rtx c_readstr (const char *str, scalar_int_mode mode, bool null_terminated_p)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return a constant integer corresponding to target reading GET_MODE_BITSIZE (MODE) bits from string constant STR. If NULL_TERMINATED_P, reading stops after '\0' character, all further ones are assumed to be zero, otherwise it reads as many characters as needed.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static int target_char_cast (tree cst, char *p)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Cast a target constant CST to target CHAR and if that value fits into host char type, return zero and put that value into variable pointed to by P.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static tree builtin_save_expr (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Similar to save_expr, but assumes that arbitrary code is not executed in between the multiple evaluations. In particular, we assume that a non-addressable local variable will not be modified.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_return_addr (enum built_in_function fndecl_code, int count)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Given TEM, a pointer to a stack frame, follow the dynamic chain COUNT times to get the address of either a higher stack frame, or a return address located within it (depending on FNDECL_CODE).

gcc/builtins.c.signature: void expand_builtin_setjmp_setup (rtx buf_addr, rtx receiver_label)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Construct the leading half of a __builtin_setjmp call. Control will return to RECEIVER_LABEL. This is also called directly by the SJLJ exception handling code.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: void expand_builtin_setjmp_receiver (rtx receiver_label)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Construct the trailing part of a __builtin_setjmp call. This is also called directly by the SJLJ exception handling code. If RECEIVER_LABEL is NULL, instead contruct a nonlocal goto handler.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static void expand_builtin_longjmp (rtx buf_addr, rtx value)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: __builtin_longjmp is passed a pointer to an array of five words (not all will be used on all machines). It operates similarly to the C library function of the same name, but is more efficient. Much of the code below is copied from the handling of non-local gotos.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static inline bool more_const_call_expr_args_p (const const_call_expr_arg_iterator *iter)
static bool validate_arglist (const_tree callexpr, ...)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: This function validates the types of a function call argument list against a specified list of tree_codes. If the last specifier is a 0, that represents an ellipsis, otherwise the last specifier must be a VOID_TYPE.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_nonlocal_goto (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to __builtin_nonlocal_goto. We're passed the target label and the address of the save area.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: void expand_builtin_update_setjmp_buf (rtx buf_addr)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: __builtin_update_setjmp_buf is passed a pointer to an array of five words (not all will be used on all machines) that was passed to __builtin_setjmp. It updates the stack pointer in that block to the current value. This is also called directly by the SJLJ exception handling code.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static void expand_builtin_prefetch (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to __builtin_prefetch. For a target that does not support data prefetch, evaluate the memory address argument in case it has side effects.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx get_memory_rtx (tree exp, tree len)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Get a MEM rtx for expression EXP which is the address of an operand to be used in a string instruction (cmpstrsi, cpymemsi, ..). LEN is the maximum length of the block of memory that might be accessed or NULL if unknown.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static int apply_args_size (void)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the size required for the block returned by __builtin_apply_args, and initialize apply_args_mode.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static int apply_result_size (void)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the size required for the block returned by __builtin_apply, and initialize apply_result_mode.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx result_vector (int savep, rtx result)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Create a vector describing the result block RESULT. If SAVEP is true, the result block is used to save the values; otherwise it is used to restore the values.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_apply_args_1 (void)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Save the state required to perform an untyped call with the same arguments as were passed to the current function.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_apply_args (void)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: __builtin_apply_args returns block of memory allocated on the stack into which is stored the arg pointer, structure value address, static chain, and all the registers that might possibly be used in performing a function call. The code is moved to the start of the function so the incoming values are saved.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_apply (rtx function, rtx arguments, rtx argsize)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Perform an untyped call and save the state required to perform an untyped return of whatever value was returned by the given function.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static void expand_builtin_return (rtx result)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Perform an untyped return.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static enum type_class type_to_class (tree type)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Used by expand_builtin_classify_type and fold_builtin_classify_type.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_classify_type (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call EXP to __builtin_classify_type.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static built_in_function mathfn_built_in_2 (tree type, combined_fn fn)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return a function equivalent to FN but operating on floating-point values of type TYPE, or END_BUILTINS if no such function exists. This is purely an operation on function codes; it does not guarantee that the target actually has an implementation of the function.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static tree mathfn_built_in_1 (tree type, combined_fn fn, bool implicit_p)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return mathematic function equivalent to FN but operating directly on TYPE, if available. If IMPLICIT_P is true use the implicit builtin declaration, otherwise use the explicit declaration. If we can't do the conversion, return null.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: tree mathfn_built_in (tree type, combined_fn fn)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Like mathfn_built_in_1, but always use the implicit array.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: tree mathfn_built_in (tree type, enum built_in_function fn)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Like mathfn_built_in_1, but take a built_in_function and always use the implicit array.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: tree mathfn_built_in_type (combined_fn fn)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Return the type associated with a built in function, i.e., the one to be passed to mathfn_built_in to get the type-specific function.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: internal_fn associated_internal_fn (tree fndecl)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: If BUILT_IN_NORMAL function FNDECL has an associated internal function, return its code, otherwise return IFN_LAST. Note that this function only tests whether the function is defined in internals.def, not whether it is actually available on the target.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: internal_fn replacement_internal_fn (gcall *call)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: If CALL is a call to a BUILT_IN_NORMAL function that could be replaced on the current target by a call to an internal function, return the code of that internal function, otherwise return IFN_LAST. The caller is responsible for ensuring that any side-effects of the built-in call are dealt with correctly. E.g. if CALL sets errno, the caller must decide that the errno result isn't needed or make it available in some other way.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_mathfn_ternary (tree exp, rtx target, rtx subtarget)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to the builtin trinary math functions (fma). Return NULL_RTX if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET. SUBTARGET may be used as the target for computing one of EXP's operands.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_mathfn_3 (tree exp, rtx target, rtx subtarget)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to the builtin sin and cos math functions. Return NULL_RTX if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET. SUBTARGET may be used as the target for computing one of EXP's operands.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static enum insn_code interclass_mathfn_icode (tree arg, tree fndecl)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Given an interclass math builtin decl FNDECL and it's argument ARG return an RTL instruction code that implements the functionality. If that isn't possible or available return CODE_FOR_nothing.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_interclass_mathfn (tree exp, rtx target)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to one of the builtin math functions that operate on floating point argument and output an integer result (ilogb, isinf, isnan, etc). Return 0 if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_sincos (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to the builtin sincos math function. Return NULL_RTX if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_cexpi (tree exp, rtx target)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to the internal cexpi builtin to the sincos math function. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static tree build_call_nofold_loc (location_t loc, tree fndecl, int n, ...)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Conveniently construct a function call expression. FNDECL names the function to be called, N is the number of arguments, and the "..." parameters are the argument expressions. Unlike build_call_exr this doesn't fold the call, hence it will always return a CALL_EXPR.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_int_roundingfn (tree exp, rtx target)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to one of the builtin rounding functions gcc defines as an extension (lfloor and lceil). As these are gcc extensions we do not need to worry about setting errno to EDOM. If expanding via optab fails, lower expression to (int)(floor(x)). EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_int_roundingfn_2 (tree exp, rtx target)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to one of the builtin math functions doing integer conversion (lrint). Return 0 if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_powi (tree exp, rtx target)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand a call to the powi built-in mathematical function. Return NULL_RTX if a normal call should be emitted rather than expanding the function in-line. EXP is the expression that is a call to the builtin function; if convenient, the result should be placed in TARGET.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_strlen (tree exp, rtx target, machine_mode target_mode)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand expression EXP which is a call to the strlen builtin. Return NULL_RTX if we failed and the caller should emit a normal call, otherwise try to get the result in TARGET, if convenient.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx expand_builtin_strnlen (tree exp, rtx target, machine_mode target_mode)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Expand call EXP to the strnlen built-in, returning the result and setting it in TARGET. Otherwise return NULL_RTX on failure.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static rtx builtin_memcpy_read_str (void *data, void *, HOST_WIDE_INT offset, fixed_size_mode mode)
gcc/builtins.c.summary: Callback routine for store_by_pieces. Read GET_MODE_BITSIZE (MODE) bytes from bytes at DATA + OFFSET and return it reinterpreted as a target constant.

gcc/builtins.c.signature: static void determine_block_size (tree len, rtx len_rtx, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *min_size, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *max_size, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *probable_max_size)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx canon_reg_for_combine (rtx x, rtx reg)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_or_truncate (machine_mode mode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Return X converted to MODE. If the value is already truncated to MODE we can just return a subreg even though in the general case we would need an explicit truncation.

If other bits are being computed or if masking operations are done that select a superset of the bits in MASK, they can sometimes be ignored. Return a possibly simplified expression, but always convert X to MODE. If X is a CONST_INT, AND the CONST_INT with MASK. MODE is the mode of the result, XMODE is the mode of X, and OP_MODE says which of MODE or XMODE is preferred for simplified versions of X. The other arguments are as for force_to_mode.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx if_then_else_cond (rtx x, rtx *ptrue, rtx *pfalse)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Return nonzero if X is an expression that has one of two values depending on whether some other value is zero or nonzero. If we return zero, we set *PTRUE and *PFALSE to X.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx known_cond (rtx x, enum rtx_code cond, rtx reg, rtx val)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Return the value of expression X given the fact that condition COND is known to be true when applied to REG as its first operand and VAL as its second. gcc/combine.c.signature: static int rtx_equal_for_field_assignment_p (rtx x, rtx y, bool widen_x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: See if X and Y are equal for the purposes of seeing if we can rewrite an assignment as a field assignment.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx make_field_assignment (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: See if X, a SET operation, can be rewritten as a bit-field assignment. Return that assignment if so. We only handle the most common cases.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx apply_distributive_law (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: See if X is of the form (+ (* a c) (* b c)) and convert to (* (+ a b) c) if so.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx distribute_and_simplify_rtx (rtx x, int n)

However, if some of the operands are the same or inverses of each other, simplifications will result. For example, (and (ior A B) (not B)) can occur as the result of expanding a bit field assignment. When we apply the distributive law to this, we get (ior (and (A (not B))) (and (B (not B)))), which then simplifies to (and (A (not B))). Note that no checks happen on the validity of applying the inverse distributive law. This is pointless since we can do it in the few places where this routine is called. N is the index of the term that is decomposed (the arithmetic operation, i.e. (+ A B) in the first example above). !N is the index of the term that is distributed, i.e. of C in the first example above.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int_1 (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Simplify a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from (and VAROP (const_int CONSTOP)). Otherwise, return NULL_RTX.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int (rtx x, scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.c.summary: We have X, a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from X. Otherwise, return X. If X is zero, we are to always construct the equivalent form.

gcc/combine.c.summary: Given a REG X of mode XMODE, compute which bits in X can be nonzero. We don't care about bits outside of those defined in MODE. We DO care about all the bits in MODE, even if XMODE is smaller than MODE. For most X this is simply GET_MODE_MASK (GET_MODE (MODE)), but if X is a shift, AND, or zero_extract, we can do better.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx reg_num_sign_bit_copies_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned int *result)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Given a reg X of mode XMODE, return the number of bits at the high-order end of X that are known to be equal to the sign bit. X will be used in mode MODE; the returned value will always be between 1 and the number of bits in MODE.

gcc/combine.c.signature: unsigned int extended_count (const_rtx x, machine_mode mode, int unsignedp)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Return the number of "extended" bits there are in X, when interpreted as a quantity in MODE whose signedness is indicated by UNSIGNEDP. For unsigned quantities, this is the number of high-order zero bits. For signed quantities, this is the number of copies of the sign bit minus 1. In both case, this function returns the number of "spare" bits. For example, if two quantities for which this function returns at least 1 are added, the addition is known not to overflow. This function will always return 0 unless called during combine, which implies that it must be called from a define_split.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static int merge_outer_ops (enum rtx_code *pop0, HOST_WIDE_INT *pconst0, enum rtx_code op1, HOST_WIDE_INT const1, machine_mode mode, int *pcomp_p)

We would now like to also perform OP1 with constant CONST1 (with *POP0 being done last). Return 1 if we can do the operation and update *POP0 and *PCONST0 with the resulting operation. *PCOMP_P is set to 1 if we would need to complement the innermost operand, otherwise it is unchanged. MODE is the mode in which the operation will be done. No bits outside the width of this mode matter. It is assumed that the width of this mode is smaller than or equal to HOST_BITS_PER_WIDE_INT. If *POP0 or OP1 are UNKNOWN, it means no operation is required. Only NEG, PLUS, IOR, XOR, and AND are supported. We may set *POP0 to SET if the proper result is simply *PCONST0. If the resulting operation cannot be expressed as one operation, we return 0 and do not change *POP0, *PCONST0, and *PCOMP_P.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static scalar_int_mode try_widen_shift_mode (enum rtx_code code, rtx op, int count, scalar_int_mode orig_mode, scalar_int_mode mode, enum rtx_code outer_code, HOST_WIDE_INT outer_const)
gcc/combine.c.summary: A helper to simplify_shift_const_1 to determine the mode we can perform the shift in. The original shift operation CODE is performed on OP in ORIG_MODE. Return the wider mode MODE if we can perform the operation in that mode. Return ORIG_MODE otherwise. We can also assume that the result of the shift is subject to operation OUTER_CODE with operand OUTER_CONST.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const_1 (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int orig_count)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by ORIG_COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. Return NULL_RTX if we cannot simplify it. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const (rtx x, enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int count)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. If we cannot simplify it, return X or, if it is NULL, synthesize the expression with simplify_gen_binary. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static int recog_for_combine_1 (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.c.summary: A subroutine of recog_for_combine. See there for arguments and return value.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static bool change_zero_ext (rtx pat)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Change every ZERO_EXTRACT and ZERO_EXTEND of a SUBREG that can be expressed as an AND and maybe an LSHIFTRT, to that formulation. Return whether anything was so changed.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static int recog_for_combine (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Like recog, but we receive the address of a pointer to a new pattern. We try to match the rtx that the pointer points to. If that fails, we may try to modify or replace the pattern, storing the replacement into the same pointer object. Modifications include deletion or addition of CLOBBERs. If the instruction will still not match, we change ZERO_EXTEND and ZERO_EXTRACT to the equivalent AND and perhaps LSHIFTRT patterns, and try with that (and undo if that fails). PNOTES is a pointer to a location where any REG_UNUSED notes added for the CLOBBERs are placed. The value is the final insn code from the pattern ultimately matched, or -1.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Like gen_lowpart_general but for use by combine. In combine it is not possible to create any new pseudoregs. However, it is safe to create invalid memory addresses, because combine will try to recognize them and all they will do is make the combine attempt fail. If for some reason this cannot do its job, an rtx (clobber (const_int 0)) is returned. An insn containing that will not be recognized.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_compare_const (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode mode, rtx op0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Try to simplify a comparison between OP0 and a constant OP1, where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested, into a (CODE OP0 const0_rtx) form. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. POP1 may be updated.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_comparison (enum rtx_code code, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Simplify a comparison between *POP0 and *POP1 where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. *POP0 and POP1 may be updated. It is possible that we might detect that a comparison is either always true or always false. However, we do not perform general constant folding in combine, so this knowledge isn't useful. Such tautologies should have been detected earlier. Hence we ignore all such cases.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static int count_rtxs (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Utility function for record_value_for_reg. Count number of rtxs in X.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void update_table_tick (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Utility function for following routine. Called when X is part of a value being stored into last_set_value. Sets last_set_table_tick for each register mentioned. Similar to mention_regs in cse.c

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void record_value_for_reg (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn, rtx value)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Record that REG is set to VALUE in insn INSN. If VALUE is zero, we are saying that the register is clobbered and we no longer know its value. gcc/combine.c.signature: static void record_dead_and_set_regs_1 (rtx dest, const_rtx setter, void *data)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void record_dead_and_set_regs (rtx_insn *insn)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static bool reg_truncated_to_mode (machine_mode mode, const_rtx x)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static bool record_truncated_value (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: If X is a hard reg or a subreg record the mode that the register is accessed in. For non-TARGET_TRULY_NOOP_TRUNCATION targets we might be able to turn a truncate into a subreg using this information. Return true if traversing X is complete.

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void record_truncated_values (rtx *loc, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static rtx get_last_value (const_rtx x)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void reg_dead_at_p_1 (rtx dest, const_rtx x, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void mark_used_regs_combine (rtx x)
gcc/combine.c.summary: Note hard registers in X that are used.

gcc/combine.c.summary: For each register (hardware or pseudo) used within expression X, if its death is in an instruction with luid between FROM_LUID (inclusive) and TO_INSN (exclusive), put a REG_DEAD note for that register in the list headed by PNOTES. gcc/combine.c.signature: static int reg_bitfield_target_p (rtx x, rtx body)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static void distribute_notes (rtx notes, rtx_insn *from_insn, rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx elim_i2, rtx elim_i1, rtx elim_i0)

gcc/combine.c.signature: static bool unmentioned_reg_p (rtx equiv, rtx expr)
